title: Quantization technical review - Aurum Labs
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a technical deep dive with Aurum Labs to align on quantization strategy for their 13B/70B inference workloads. Discussed INT8/FP8 tradeoffs, GPTQ and AWQ toolchains, expected accuracy regression windows, and runtime impacts on latency and throughput. Agreed to run a pilot quantization benchmark using Aurum's eval set in Redwood Dedicated and Private modes; action items include sharing benchmark template, security docs, and scheduling an on-prem pilot window.
action_items: Miguel - run baseline INT8/GPTQ + AWQ runs on 13B model and share results (due 2027-08-18)
Tom - provide representative eval prompts + dataset link (due 2027-08-13)
Alyssa - share security docs (SOC2, VPC guide) and pricing for Dedicated pilot (due 2027-08-12)
Priya - confirm internal compliance reviewers and availability for on-prem pilot week (due 2027-08-16)
next_steps: Redwood to run quantized benchmarks (INT8/GPTQ and AWQ) on customer's eval set
Customer to evaluate quality delta and provide failure cases
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa (Redwood AE), Miguel (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood SE), Tom (Aurum ML), Priya (Aurum CTO), Liam (Aurum Platform)

---
AUTO-GENERATED SUMMARY (may be imperfect):
- High level: quantization options and expected quality/perf tradeoffs for 13B/70B family; pilot plan for Dedicated/Private runs.

---
Transcript:
[00:00] Alyssa: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alyssa from redwood inference. today miguel and samir are gonna walk through quantization tradeoffs and runtime impacts, we'll leave time for your deck and questions.
[00:12] Tom: thanks, yeah we've been tracking cost on our 13B fleet and also looking at some 70 b experiments. main goals: cut token cost by ~3-5x and keep qa and NLU accuracy within a small delta.
[00:22] Miguel: perfect. quick question on your accuracy SLOs — is the tolerable regression like 1-2% absolute or relative?
[00:28] Priya: ideally <2% absolute on our main intent classification and <1% on key slot filling. anything more and product team will push back.
[00:37] Miguel: ok that gives us a target. overview: we typically evaluate three families — FP8 (if supported), INT8 per-channel (quant) using GPTQ toolchain, and AWQ (asymmetric weight quant) which has some speed benefits. each has very different accuracy vs perf curve.
[00:52] Samir: also want to call out runtime implications — INT8 can be very fast on kernels that support it but you need quantized kernels and sometimes a different memory layout; AWQ often reduces memory more and can improve batching density but some toolchains produce slightly higher regressions on certain instruction-following tasks.
[01:10] Tom: we've seen that with a third-party aud model where gptq produced weird hallucination spikes on longer contexts, so that's a real concern.
[01:18] Miguel: yeah context length interaction is important. we also need to consider KV cache handling — when you quantize weights, KV cache (the cached key/value activations) size doesn't always shrink proportionally, so streaming latency for long dialogs can still be dominated by KV IO.
[01:34] Liam: question — if we go with Dedicated vs Private on prem, how much of the perf delta is infra vs quantization?
[01:41] Samir: good question — infra plays a role mostly on IO and GPU interconnect. Dedicated (managed) gives predictable GPU kernel support and tuned drivers; on-prem variation depends on your stack, e.g., whether you're on A100s with proper ampere drivers or on H100s which have different fp8/ptx characteristics.
[01:58] Priya: we plan on using H100s for critical workloads and older A100s for cost tier. can redwood handle mixed-device routing?
[02:06] Miguel: yes, smart routing can direct requests by model variant and hardware; we can set policies so low-priority traffic runs on cheaper A100s with INT8 and higher SLO traffic uses H100 with FP8 or fp16.
[02:16] Tom: for toolchain — do you recommend GPTQ or AWQ for our 13B? we've heard AWQ is faster but less stable on some prompts.
[02:24] Miguel: short answer: run both. GPTQ tends to preserve perplexity better for many open models but can be heavier to compute and sometimes brittle for instruction-following. AWQ often gives better memory compression and faster inference in our bench, but it's model dependent — some LLaMA-derivatives show larger deltas.
[02:38] Alyssa: can you give an example of delta we might expect?
[02:41] Samir: roughly speaking, for 13B: INT8/GPTQ might give 0.5-1.5% absolute regression on classification tasks; AWQ could be 0.8-2.5% in worst cases. FP8 (where supported) can be sub-0.5% but needs hardware/kernel support and may cost more.
[02:58] Tom: that's in line with what we've seen. latency wise — what's the per-token latency bump for INT8 vs fp16 on H100?
[03:05] Miguel: on H100 with optimized kernels we see INT8 latency comparable to fp16, sometimes slightly lower due to smaller memory footprint and better cache locality. On A100, INT8 kernels might not be as optimized, so fp16 could be faster. these numbers vary by sequence length and batch size.
[03:21] Priya: you mentioned sequence length. our main workload has 1-3k tokens in session, avg 900. KV cache becomes large. do you have suggestions?
[03:31] Samir: two levers: prefix/KV caching and chunked generation. caching the prefix (common system prompts) can reduce repeated compute; for long sessions consider segmenting KV to disk-backed caches in Private deployment, but that affects latency. also, batching policy — continuous batching helps throughput but may add tail latency.
[03:47] Tom: what's Redwood's approach to controlling batching vs tail latency?
[03:51] Miguel: policy-driven. you set latency SLOs per route; runtime uses predictive batching and will only batch up to a deadline to meet SLO. for Dedicated we can tune batch windows tighter. for Private/on-prem we give knobs and recommended defaults.
[04:05] Priya: security — if we do on-prem, we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. is that supported?
[04:11] Alyssa: yes; for Private we offer KMS integration and audit logs, SOC2 docs we'll share. for on-prem there are options for customer-managed KMS or HSM. i'll drop the security package link.
[04:21] Tom: one pain point: when we tried GPTQ the conversion tooling changed tokenization subtly which caused some alignment issues in downstream extractors. any mitigation?
[04:30] Miguel: that's usually from differences in normalization or from using different tokenizers during conversion. mitigation: keep tokenizer artifact identical, include tokenization tests in the eval harness. also generate token-level diffs as part of the benchmark so we can see where it diverges.
[04:44] Samir: we also recommend a small set of targeted prompts (edge cases) — instruction-following, multi-turn context, numeric reasoning — that frequently reveal regressions. include these in your eval set.
[04:55] Tom: ok we'll put that together.
[04:58] Priya: curious about fallback strategy — if quantized variant fails quality checks in production, what is the failover?
[05:05] Miguel: we support automatic rollbacks and multi-variant routing. if AWQ/INT8 fails QA thresholds, we can route traffic to fp16/fp32 variant. Redwood's rollout system supports canary and A/B with automatic quality gating if you feed back eval metrics.
[05:20] Tom: do you have a recommended threshold for gating?
[05:22] Samir: commonly teams use 1% absolute for critical classifiers, or 2% for less critical flows. but depends on your risk tolerance.
[05:30] Priya: let's talk about bench specifics — miguel what will you run?
[05:33] Miguel: we'll run baseline fp16 on both H100 and A100, then GPTQ INT8 and AWQ for the 13B model. metrics: token latency P50/P95, throughput (tokens/sec), memory footprint, and quality metrics (classification accuracy, exact-match for slots, perplexity). we'll also produce per-prompt deltas so you can triage failures.
[05:51] Tom: timeframe?
[05:53] Miguel: if we get your eval set by monday (2027-08-13), we can have initial runs by thursday and a full report by next tuesday (2027-08-18).
[06:02] Priya: we'll try to turn it around.
[06:05] Alyssa: i'll share the benchmark template and the security docs after the call. also pricing for a 2-week Dedicated pilot and an on-prem pilot quote.
[06:13] Liam: on-prem pilot — what does that look like operationally? 
[06:17] Samir: usually we do a two-stage process: first validate infra (drivers, cuda, networking), then run calibration quantization (GPTQ/AWQ) inside your environment; we can do remote pairing and a short onsite if needed. the critical piece is ensuring the environment uses the same kernels we bench on.
[06:34] Tom: any gotchas on mixed-device clusters? we've got heterogenous pool with H100 + A100 nodes and some 80G vs 40G interconnects.
[06:43] Miguel: network fabric matters for KV-heavy workloads. for long context streaming, PCIe/NVLink topology and host-to-device bandwidth affect tail latency. we can route requests to device types appropriately; it's also possible to pin low-latency SLO traffic to H100s.
[06:57] Priya: are there licensing or model provenance concerns with GPTQ/AWQ when using third-party toolchains?
[07:05] Alyssa: generally toolchains are open-source but check model licenses; some models have restrictions on derivatives — we'll include a short note in the security package.
[07:13] Tom: any sample numbers you can share from previous customers?
[07:16] Miguel: anonymized: a 13B family model in Dedicated on H100 showed 2.8x cost reduction with INT8/GPTQ with 0.9% absolute accuracy regression; AWQ produced 3.6x cost reduction with 1.4% regression in worst-case prompts but improved throughput by ~20%. your mileage will vary.
[07:37] Priya: okay good. let's capture next steps.
[07:40] Alyssa: recap: 1) tom to share eval set; 2) miguel/engineering to run INT8/GPTQ and AWQ runs on H100/A100; 3) redwood to share security and pricing; 4) schedule bench review 2027-08-20.
[07:58] Tom: that works. thanks.
[08:01] Priya: thanks everyone.
[08:03] Alyssa: thanks all — we'll follow up via email with links to the spreadsheet and next steps.

[08:10] (meeting end)
